title.narrative: IDS FUND FOR ETHIOPIA: LEAVING NO ONE BEHIND – THE INTERNAL DISPLACEMENT SOLUTIONS FUND (IDSF)

description.narrative:
Ethiopia faces one of the most complex human mobility environments in the world, with multiple conflicts and disasters that have led to widespread displacement. As identified through Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM), there are 4.39 million IDPs in 3,393 accessible sites. Conflict has been the primary cause of displacement for 2.9 million IDPs followed by drought (810,855). During the same reporting period, DTM identified 3,238,803 returning IDPs across 2,754 assessed, accessible villages. The highest assessed returning IDP caseloads nationwide were in Amhara (1,422,074), Tigray (1,256,297) and Afar (194,968), while Somali region recorded only 2,973 returning IDPs. There, protracted displacement is a major issue. Despite the high number of IDPs and increasingly protracted nature of displacement in the country, limited efforts have been made to foster conditions conducive to the IDPs' (re-)integration, such as expanding basic social infrastructure and creating a peaceful environment together with the hosting communities. Additionally, while limited progress has been made on achieving solutions, agreed assessment tools are lacking to determine when IDPs have achieved a durable solution. Persistent conflicts and an increasing number of disasters have raised concerns about the deterioration of social cohesion due to increased marginalization, stigmatization, and discrimination. Furthermore, livelihood coupled with restricted movement, reduced access to markets and land, disruption of the labor market, increase in prices, has been hindered. Importantly, sharply defined gender roles in small and remote areas leave a double burden to females within displaced communities. Supporting the livelihoods of IDPs and returnees by supporting progress towards durable solutions is essential. This would include vulnerable women, youth and those affected by gender-based violence (GBV).
In the three northern regions, protection monitoring, and intention surveys indicate that recent returns mostly took place in North Wollo, Wag Himra, and North Gondar regions of Amhara, North-West, Central and Eastern zones of Tigray, Kilibati/Zone 2 of Afar. Return counselling, registration exercises, and intention surveys indicate the IDPs wish is to return and resume their lives and livelihood activities. The latest Protection Monitoring and Solutions survey (May 2023) indicated that the main protection issues faced by IDP returnees are (1) houses, lands and properties destroyed, (2) lack of services (school, health, market, civil registration, grain mill, and WASH), (3) inflation, (4) loss of belongings, (5) lack of access to financial institutions, and (6) missing family members. Nine out of 10 Kl reported observing signs of distress among the populations. 64% of KI reported IDP returnees are the most affected, while women are the group showing the most signs of distress. Access to documentation was reported as a significant issue for (1) checkpoints, (2) travel restriction, (3) access to basic services, (4) opening bank accounts, and (5) finding employment. One out of two respondents in all the visited locations reported the destruction and lack of civil registration offices as the main barrier to having legal documentation.
The UN country team has only recently started entering into joint Durable Solutions Programming. Currently, some of the consortium partners for the IDSF project, currently collaborating under a four year joint project: Strengthening Resilience of Disaster Affected Communities through Durable Solutions in Oromia and Somali Regions of Ethiopia (IOM, UN-Habitat, FAO).
The basic assumption is that none of the partners have the capacities nor the tools to develop solutions pathways for addressing the scale of the challenges centered around protracted and recent displacement in Ethiopia caused by overlaps of internal, specific local and disaster induced conflicts.
The Piper Report of the United Nations Secretary General’s Special Adviser on Solutions to Internal Displacement concludes that “the pivot towards development informed solutions at scale has not yet been internalised, with the UN mainly working in project mode towards solutions with short-term funding from partners being an impediment to supporting systemic change. The narrative on UN value add on the agenda needs strengthening, with more focus on the convening role, policy development and strategy. Ongoing programming efforts could further inform learning processes to bring opportunities to scale”.
The Piper Report recommends utilizing the opportunity of the first funding round of the IDSF as an important opportunity to accelerate efforts and in particular address capacity gaps in state and federal level Government structures in the context of the expected IDP proclamation and the UN reform agenda towards solutions pathways rather than singular and agency specific interventions.
